items.note: Describes Udaipur as a marginal, desolate-looking town of eight thousand people.
items.gloss: A marginalised, desolate-looking town of eight thousand people, which for several decades had wanted to say something.

items.note: Places this Udaipur 150 km from Bhopal, the capital of Madhya Pradesh.
items.gloss: This Udaipur is at a distance of a hundred and fifty kilometres from Bhopal, the capital of Madhya Pradesh.

items.note: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, the Afghan Dost Mohammad Khan came to this region and took service in a small Rajput jagir near Bairasia, later becoming master of an old Gond principality.
items.gloss: In 1707 Aurangzeb died far in the south; in the confusion in Delhi in the following years an Afghan named Dost Mohammad Khan left Delhi and was first seen in this region. He got service in a small Rajput jagir near Berasia, 40 km from Bhopal, and through deceit and attacks soon became the new master of an old Gond principality.

items.note: After independence Udaipur remained untouched by the hopes of the new country and stayed desolate, its old grandeur unexamined.
items.gloss: But Udaipur remained untouched for decades by the hopes born in the country after independence. If independence brought a new dawn, it never reached the walls of Udaipur's fallen fort. It remained a desolation wrapped in sadness; no one felt a need to look into its ancient grandeur.

items.note: Udaipur's bus stand junction: tarmac road runs 16 km to Ganj Basoda (nearest railway station), another 22 km to Mandi Bamora; Udaipur lies in this tehsil of Vidisha district; Kurwai seat covers it.
items.gloss: A dusty, ruined three-way junction whose tarmac road in front joins Ganj Basoda 16 km away. Ganj Basoda is the nearest railway station and a small trading town; Udaipur falls in this tehsil of Vidisha district. The other road turns 90 degrees and goes 22 km to Mandi Bamora, the second railway station. On this road, seven km from Mandi Bamora, is Kurwai, within whose assembly constituency Udaipur falls.

items.note: Kurwai, like Bhopal, was a small principality for two hundred years under another Afghan family related to the family that seized Bhopal.
items.gloss: Like Bhopal, Kurwai too had been for two hundred years a small principality in the possession of another Afghan family, whose relatives belonged to the family that took Bhopal. Abida Begum, daughter of the Afghan chief who held Bhopal, was married to the holder of Kurwai.

items.note: Udaipur's dark womb holds much, and its story lies on countless inscriptions.
items.gloss: But in Udaipur's own dark womb much is contained, eager to introduce itself. Its story is on countless inscriptions.

items.note: The roughly 300 m lane has decades-old stone shops built of Udaipur's own stone with almost no cement or bricks; old stone doorways visible in closed houses.
items.gloss: On both sides of this lane, about three hundred metres long, are decades-old shops built of stone: cloth, grocery, sweets. These shops are made of stones found in Udaipur itself, with almost no cement or bricks. In many old, closed houses stone doors of the old period are clearly visible. Everything here was of stone.

items.note: At the lane's end a huge old stone gate leads to the Nilkantheshvar Mahadev temple, among the finest monuments of the Paramara period; the main east door has long been shut.
items.gloss: At the end of the lane a very old, huge stone gate is seen, on whose other side is the Nilkantheshvar Mahadev temple, one of the finest monuments of this region from the time of the Paramara kings. That narrow, suffocating lane is the only way to the door at the back of the temple. The temple's main east-facing door has been closed for who knows how long.

items.note: Udaipur is a gram panchayat in an area rich in stone quarries.
items.gloss: It is a gram panchayat. This condition should not be at all in this area rich in stone quarries.

items.note: Visitors go straight in for worship and abhisheka of Nilkantheshvar Mahadev in the sanctum, bringing prayers for jobs, marriages, court cases and wealth.
items.gloss: Visiting Indians were interested only in the temple, and not even the temple but Nilkantheshvar Mahadev seated in its sanctum. People went straight in. They did worship and abhisheka, and came out hanging one more kind of the poison of their endless wishes on Bholenath's neck.

items.note: Few visitors notice the temple's architecture or its real history; they photograph it and leave.
items.gloss: Very few people paid attention to the temple's astonishing architecture. Almost none looked into its real history. All came out of the temple and left Udaipur without wasting time.

items.note: On both sides of the temple complex are Paramara-era constructions: old houses of huge carved stone; narrow lanes were once wide roads that shrank through unlawful occupation after the Paramaras.
items.gloss: On both sides of the temple's finest precinct are astonishing constructions made in the time of the Paramara kings. Old houses built by arranging massive carved stones. The narrow lanes too must once have been fairly wide, straight, clean roads, which after the Paramaras shrank and became narrow through unlawful occupation.

items.note: The Paramara kingdom's northern border extended to Udaipur, where Kalachuri territory began; its border position made it strategically important.
items.gloss: From within Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan, the northern limit of the Paramara kingdom extended up to Udaipur here. From here the Kalachuri territory began. Being on the border, Udaipur must have been strategically very important for the Paramaras, as its thousand-year-old development and expansion also show.

items.note: Bija Mandal, a residential-looking complex whose original building must have been grand; a basement-like room has a doorway like the old temple's, about as old.
items.gloss: Instead of going into the temple we first went into a building that is called Bija Mandal there. From outside it is a residential complex like ordinary village houses, but only inside does one understand that the original building must once have been very grand. The door of one of its basement-like rooms is just like that of an old temple, about as old as the temple.

items.note: One side of the doorway has a surviving eight-line Sanskrit inscription in a square stone frame; the matching frame on the other side is blank, either never inscribed or scraped.
items.gloss: On one side of this door, in a splendid square stone frame, an eight-line Sanskrit inscription survives. On the other side an inscription frame of the same size is empty. Either nothing was written on it or what was written was scraped off. It does not look as if anything was written; it was clean like a blank slate.

items.note: Bija Mandal interior: sanctum-like space empty of any deity and filled with husk; two side rooms on carved pillars; later rooms on the roof; the later construction is itself four to six hundred years old.
items.gloss: If it was a temple, the deities were absent from the sanctum, and this empty space was filled with husk. On both sides of the sanctum there were two rooms, equally old, their roof's weight resting on splendid carved pillars. Some habitable rooms must have been built on the roof much later. Old and new construction is clearly visible. The new is not new either; it must be four to six hundred years old.

items.note: Family tradition: bells and gongs were sounded from Bija Mandal at the temple's fixed times of worship, abhisheka and rites, signalling the town; it may have housed a temple manager.
items.gloss: They say that once, at the fixed times of the temple's worship, abhisheka and rituals, bells and gongs were sounded from this very building. It was a notice to the whole town that it was time to come to the temple. Perhaps special signals were also given when the royal family was at the temple. In this respect it was an important institution linked to the temple's activities, possibly also used as the residence of an important person connected with temple management or ritual.

items.note: Under the Paramaras temples were also local knowledge centres and schools, as the Saraswati Kanthabharanas show; the Sabha Mandal of old Bhopal was built by Udayaditya, creator of this Udaipur.
items.gloss: Under Paramara rule temples were not limited to worship and rituals. At the local level they were also used as knowledge centres or schools. Children were taught there all the disciplines of their time. The Saraswati Kanthabharanas of Dhar, Ujjain and Mandu have been proof of this. The historic Sabha Mandal of old Bhopal in Chowk Bazaar was also built by Maharaja Udayaditya, the maker of this very Udaipur, who came after Raja Bhoj in the Paramara dynasty.

items.note: In the lanes, huge doorways in the Paramara kings' distinctive style still stand; houses pressed against them turned wide roads into narrow lanes.
items.gloss: We went into those lanes where huge doorways built in the Paramara kings' special architectural style still survive. Houses on both sides have gradually pressed very close to the ancient doorways. Therefore those old, wide, orderly roads have turned into narrow lanes.

items.note: When the Paramara splendour ended Udaipur became an orphan; after Turkish occupation of Delhi it was caught by far-reaching changes and new marks appeared on old constructions.
items.gloss: When the Paramara splendour ended, Udaipur too became an orphan. In the centuries after the occupation of Delhi by the Turks, followers of Islam, Udaipur too was caught in the changes that spread far. New marks began to appear on the old constructions.

items.note: Author guesses from ruined doorways that this was a commercial complex, a residence of an important person or an administrative office, once busy with chariots, bullock-carts and horsemen (conjecture).
items.gloss: Groping through the decayed splendour on both sides of the dusty, stony paths, we both guessed that these desolate doorways of the ruin show there must have been some commercial complexes or the residence of some very important person. It is possible they were offices connected with administration, where people from far came and went. At some time chariots, bullock-carts and horsemen must have moved here in great style.
